title: Earliest songs and the Callender uncles' family group
summary: First blues heard was St. Louis Blues at about eight; uncles played mandolin, guitar, bass and sang; father played accordion; Junk Man Rag and other repertoire.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Oh, well you've been done quite a bit of traveling. Oh yes, I did a lot of that. What's the earliest music or singing that you remember?

Well, the first blues I ever heard was St. Louis Blues. To remember, the first blues I've heard was St. Louis Blues. Then I've heard a lot of other old songs. Songs like, Who Stole a Lock Off the Hen House Door. I heard a song about Big Rock Candy Mountain. And I heard the song about K.C. John, Steamboat Bill. And another old song I used to sing around New Orleans years ago when I was a kid. He'd sing that song about Winter Night and the Junkman Rag. And all those old songs way back here. And songs, old quartet song. Old quartet used to sing songs about shots and shells are ringing on the battlefield. And another song they used to sing about when sailing over the mountain hill. Many storm and wind shall blow when Jack come home again. All those old numbers.
How old were you when you heard St. Louis Blues, Lemma?

Well, I must have been around about eight years old when I heard the St. Louis Blues. I was about eight. I had an uncle who played a mandolin. One played a guitar. And another uncle played a bass. Bass violin. And one of my uncles used to sing.
I see. What were their names?

Well, one named Fred Nan Callender. And what did he play? He played a mandolin. And the others? One named Fred Callender. He played the guitar. And you had one more? Yeah, I had another one. One they called Joseph Callender. He played a bass. And my uncle Willie Callender used to sing. Yeah, that's the four of them. And were they here in the city? Yeah, they was all around here. But they was partly raised around Plaquemine, Louisiana, out here. The road there in this piece. But they used to be here.
And did they perform just as a group themselves or would they play with other bands?
Well, no. They just had a group of themselves, you know, just brothers.
What about your father? Did he play?
Well, my father used to play accordion years ago. So they said, but I was too young to know anything about it. Because I was a baby when he died, you know. My daddy died.
What kind of songs would your uncles play? All those that you named or brothers?

Well, yeah. Those numbers I named, they used to play those numbers. St. Louis Blues. They played K.C. John. Steamboat Bill. That Oughta Get It. And they played the Junk Man Rag. And they played Shots and Shells Are Rain On The Battlefield. And they used to play I Had A Dream. I Had A Dream. And they played the... Over there. Send a word to the boys over there. They're always in World War I.
How did that Junk Man Rag go? Do you remember any words to it?

No, I can't get the words, but I know it's the air. The music of it is strange. Can you remember it this low? Yeah, mm-hmm. It goes... D-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d Can you play that on the U? Well I used to but it's been quite a while since I tried to play that. Well I can learn it. I can learn it in a couple of hours or so and I can do practice it. Junkman Rag, that's an old, old number.
